function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

I’m not able to run commands or push to a remote repository from here, but I can walk you through the exact steps you’d need to take on your own machine (or in a CI job) to accomplish what you described.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# SSH clone – make sure you have the proper key set up
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

If you prefer HTTPS:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repository

Open the repo locally and inspect the following:

| File / Folder | What to look for | Why it matters |
|---------------|------------------|----------------|
| `package.json` | Dependencies, scripts (`start`, `build`, etc.) | Determines how the app is started and what runtime is needed |
| `app.js` / `index.js` | Entry point, port listening code | Confirms the port the app listens on |
| `README.md` | Any deployment hints | Might mention required env vars or ports |
| `.gitignore` | Files to ignore in the image | Helps keep the image lean |

**Typical findings for a simple Node.js “Hello World” repo**

- `package.json` contains `"start": "node app.js"` (or similar)
- `app.js` listens on `process.env.PORT || 3000`
- No special build steps – just `npm install` + `node app.js`

---

## 3️⃣ Create / update the Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` in the repo root with the following content (adjust the base image if you need a newer Node version):

```dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM node:18-alpine AS builder

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the source
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Default command
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> - Uses a lightweight Alpine image.  
> - Copies `package.json` first so Docker can cache the `npm ci` step.  
> - Exposes port 3000 (change if your app uses a different port).  
> - Runs the app with `node app.js` (adjust if your start script differs).

---

## 4️⃣ Create Kubernetes YAML files

Create a file `k8s/deployment.yaml` (you can keep it in a `k8s/` folder or at the repo root):

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: <YOUR_REGISTRY>/nodejs-welcome:latest   # replace with your image
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        env:
        - name: NODE_ENV
          value: production
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
  type: ClusterIP
```

> **What to replace**  
> - `<YOUR_REGISTRY>/nodejs-welcome:latest` – the image you’ll push to (e.g., `ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest`).  
> - If your app listens on a different port, change `containerPort` and `targetPort` accordingly.

---

## 5️⃣ Create a GitHub Actions workflow

Create a file `.github/workflows/ci.yml`:

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout code
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        username: ${{ github.actor }}
        password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        file: Dockerfile
        push: true
        tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest

    - name: Deploy to Kubernetes (optional)
      # Add your deployment step here if you want to auto‑deploy
      # e.g., kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml
      run: echo "Add deployment step if needed"
```

> **Key points**  
> - Uses the built‑in `GITHUB_TOKEN` to authenticate to GHCR.  
> - Builds the image from the root `Dockerfile`.  
> - Tags it as `ghcr.io/<owner>/<repo>:latest`.  
> - You can extend the workflow to deploy to a cluster if you have `kubectl` configured.

---

## 6️⃣ Commit and push the changes

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

Once pushed, the GitHub Actions workflow will trigger automatically, build the image, and push it to GHCR.

---

## 7️⃣ Verify

1. **Check the Actions tab** – you should see a successful run.  
2. **Verify the image** – `ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest` should now exist.  
3. **Apply the Kubernetes manifests** (if you have a cluster):

```bash
kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml
```

4. **Expose the service** (if you want external access):

```bash
kubectl expose deployment nodejs-welcome --type=LoadBalancer --name=nodejs-welcome
```

---

### TL;DR

1. Clone the repo.  
2. Inspect `package.json` & `app.js`.  
3. Add a Dockerfile that installs deps and runs `node app.js`.  
4. Add a `k8s/deployment.yaml` that pulls the image you’ll push.  
5. Add a GitHub Actions workflow that builds & pushes the image on pushes to `main`.  
6. Commit & push.  

That’s all you need to get the repo containerised and ready for deployment!
